item.description:
A grid now has as many blocks as there are windows in it, and keeps it that way as windows come and go.

A workspace holding a single window could show four or six blocks when you dragged something into it. Windows of an app you had quit with them still open went on being counted, for as long as Deckz kept running. They are now let go of the moment the app quits.

Closing an app's last window — a Finder window with Command-W, a screenshot editor you have finished with — used to leave its block behind until you switched workspace. Deckz now notices, and the windows that are left take the room back straight away. The same happens when you send a window to another workspace: the grid or cascade it came from closes up behind it. Workspaces with zones you drew are left as they are, since those blocks stay where you put them.

A second window joining a lone one now sits beside it rather than above it. Rows you once chose by dragging a window to the lower half of the screen were remembered for good, so every window that turned up afterwards split the screen top and bottom. They are now forgotten once the workspace is back to one window. Dragging still chooses the rows whenever you want something else.

Dragging a window that had opened in a workspace on its own no longer offers one block too many.

And sending the window you are typing in to another workspace now takes the keyboard off it, so what you type next does not go to a window you can no longer see. It goes to the window you used last in the workspace you are looking at, or nowhere if that workspace is now empty.

A window sent to a workspace could disappear for good.

It happened when the same application was running twice at once — an ordinary browser, say, beside a copy of itself started by a development tool. Deckz looked at only one of the two, so the window in front of you could be one it had never heard of. Sending it to a workspace put it away, switching back brought nothing, and recovering off-screen windows could not reach it either. It was gone until you quit the application.

Deckz now looks at every copy of an application that is running, so the window comes back where you left it.

A copy with no icon in the Dock is still left alone. Those windows are not ones you can see or reach, and giving one a place in a grid would leave a gap nothing fills.

If a window is stranded from before, it comes back the first time you visit its workspace after installing this.

Switching to a workspace now moves the keyboard there.

Press a workspace's key and you can type straight away. Before, the keyboard stayed on whatever you were last using — including a window that had just been put away — so what you typed went somewhere you could not see.

The window that takes it is the one you used most recently in that workspace. Carrying a workspace to the next screen takes the keyboard with it too.

A workspace with nothing in it hands the keyboard to Deckz instead, so a keystroke cannot reach a window that is off screen. The menu bar goes on showing whichever app was there before — Deckz has no menu bar of its own — but the keys stop going anywhere until you open something or switch away.

This only happens when you ask for it. When Deckz changes workspace on its own, because an app opened a window somewhere else or because a screen was plugged in, the keyboard stays where it is.

Several things that moved windows without being asked are fixed as well.

Plugging a screen in or out no longer empties your hidden workspaces onto one screen. It used to happen a second after the change, and the windows kept whatever size they were given on the way, so a window could come back narrower every time its workspace crossed between a wide screen and the laptop.

Windows brought back from off screen now land on the screen with the menu bar, rather than on whichever screen sits furthest to the left, and one that is already the right size is left alone.

Opening an app whose windows live in another workspace no longer rearranges the screen you are not working on. That workspace comes up where you are.

The badge in the menu bar names the workspace that is really on screen, instead of the one that was asked for when the switch did not happen.

Changing the number of rows in a grid works again, and a window that opens into the workspace in front of you is given a place in it.

Deckz now works with more than one screen.

Each screen shows its own workspace. Switching workspace on one leaves the other alone — until now, changing workspace anywhere put away the windows on every screen, so the second one went blank and stayed blank.

The menu bar shows one badge per screen, left to right in the order the screens sit in front of you. The filled badge is the screen your pointer is on.

A workspace remembers which screen it belongs to. Press its key and it comes up there. If it is already showing on another screen, the keyboard goes to it rather than dragging it across — a workspace is only ever on one screen, and moving it somewhere you were not looking would leave that screen empty.

Option-Shift-Tab carries the workspace you are on to the next screen, and it stays there: through switching away and back, through quitting and reopening, and through unplugging the screen and plugging it in again. The screen it left goes back to whatever it was showing before.

Unplug a screen and its workspaces are still reachable on the one that is left. Plug it back in and they return to it.

The first time you open this version with two screens attached, Deckz gives each screen a workspace to show and brings that workspace's windows onto it, so some windows will move once. After that a workspace only changes screen when you move it.

With a single screen nothing is different.

Deckz can now report its own problems.

"Report a Problem…" in the menu opens a bug report with the version you are running and your macOS version already filled in. Those are the two things a report is usually missing, and the two nobody should have to go and look up.

The website gained a page about installing, which explains why macOS refuses an early build the first time and what to do about it — including which button in that dialog not to press.

Settings now says who makes Deckz.

Creating a workspace now asks which key it answers to.

"New Workspace" offers the keys that are still free; pick one and the workspace is reachable straight away — ⌥ and the key switches to it, ⌥⇧ and the key sends the focused window there. Before, a new workspace arrived as a draft that could not be reached at all until you opened it and found the key picker inside.

Give it a layout afterwards, or leave it without one: a workspace with no layout still groups windows, it just does not rearrange them.

If this is the first version you let update itself, that part worked.

Deckz now keeps itself up to date.

It looks for a new version when it starts, and once a day after that. When one exists it tells you what changed and asks; nothing is installed without you saying so. There is a "Check for Updates…" item in the menu for when you would rather ask than wait, and a switch in Settings → General if you would rather it install on its own.

Updating restarts Deckz. If you have windows in workspaces you are not looking at, those windows come back to the main display when it reopens — so the update window tells you how many will move before anything happens.

This version has to be installed by hand, the same way you installed the last one. No version before this one has any way to update itself, which is the thing this version adds. From here on it is a button.
